title: The Conn band selling school bands in Mississippi; Charlie Wagner
summary: Charlie Wagner and the group played school concerts to sign up students for rented instruments, which started Mississippi high-school bands, and musicians later became teachers.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: And then... We went up to Jackson, Mississippi. I think Al Hesma was with us. Al's still alive, I think. Yeah, sure is. Was up by Doug Chopper. And, uh... It was Naya Weinberg, Johnny Reingar, Eddie Powers... Charlie Wagner... You didn't know Charlie Wagner. You heard of him. Yeah, the name is... Charlie Wagner... Was... Without a doubt... The greatest... Manipulator in the world. He could... He could talk you into... Fly into the moon. Which he probably was gonna do that. He invented the Wagner phone. The Wagner phone was gonna take the place of the atom bomb. You'd hit a certain note on the Wagner phone... And everything would explode.

You'd hit a certain note on the Wagner phone... And everything would explode. You know the old glass... Vibrations. The Wagner phone was gonna do it. Without a doubt... He finally, after he gave up music... He became a professor down at one of the high schools down there. The one that was... I think it was Nichols. ! Where they had the Confederate flag. I mean, they had a lot of trouble down there with the Confederate flag. And, uh... Because the colored people didn't like the Confederate flag. So he left the teaching business. Well, he got to be a teacher from... I'm getting ahead of myself. He got to be a teacher from... Up in Mississippi. Where we used to go into a school at lunchtime and play a concert. Some of them were a con company. The manager used to fly up there. Park the thing in the river or something like that to get the way he's going. He'd get up there and get nothing. We used to... He'd get up there and he'd talk the service organizations to underwrite the... bass, trombones, baritones and big instruments. Five dollars a week. And they were satisfying them. and they were satisfying them. So we go and we play a concert at the school and this was around 19, maybe 31, maybe before that, maybe 26 or 27. How would you all like to have a band like this? Oh, right, right, right, right. Okay, now you can have a band like this but not right away. What we're going to do, we're going to pass out slips of papers and we want you to write your name on it, what instrument you would like to play and your mother's and your father's name, your telephone number and your house address. And in the afternoon when they'd get finished, these guys would go around and they'd call on these people. And that's how they were teaching them. They were renting a clarinet for $6 a month and if they didn't like it they'd get it back and they'd rent it to somebody else for $6 a month. They had a tuba up there that they rented out for $5 a month. That thing must have been rented 50 times. And that's how the name band, I mean the high school bands up in Mississippi got started. Well now, what music would you play for them when you played the country? We would play the popular music that we knew how to play. Yeah. You know what I'm saying? So you might be playing even by ear? Yeah. Could be. I could just see those kids. Well we know the things by heart. We have to play them. But... I'm not used to wrestling in college at the beginning. And that's how several of these guys became professors. In fact, for a while you could become a professor without a college degree in the city of New Orleans. What happened to a lot of musicians, I mean I know, Louis Macenta, Henry Newfield, and several guys, I can't think of their names, but they were taking summer courses at Loyola to get credits so that they would have enough so they would be legitimate to be able to teach in the public school system. I mean, Newfield, Newfield, he used to go up there every summer to take courses, teaching them how to play violin. He was never going to play violin, but they showed them how to hold the violin. It's the same thing with the Navy. When you graduate in the second class Navy musician, that means that you can conduct the Star Spangled Banner. You're able to conduct the Star Spangled Banner. I haven't had a degree as a second class musician. Well, Charlie Wagner, through his life, he was teaching in high school and so forth and so on. He left the high school and he went and got into the library of Jefferson Parish. And he was the director of the libraries in Jefferson Parish. I saw him one day, and we worked together a long time, we knew each other well. Patrick, you need publicity for your, I was president of the Floral Trail. You need publicity for your Floral Trail, we gotta get newspaper publicity. And I need publicity for my library. He says, I've got an idea. He says, I've got a plant, I've got a rose plant that we could plant it. And this plant is called the Jean Lafitte Rose. I said, well, what does that mean? He said, well, the Jean Lafitte Rose, when you plant it and it blooms, it's white. And if the British are coming, it turns red.
